title: The Safety of Objects
full_review:
"The Safety of Objects" (IFC) follows the travails of characters in four neighboring households, only to conclude on a falsely upbeat note. Were it not for the deliberate, horrifying choice made by Glenn Close's central character, the film could be praised as a sensitive exploration of mostly age-related problems of the interconnected parents and youngsters. But her character's actions put the whole film in a different, negative light.

By continuous cross-cutting we are introduced to four families in adjacent suburban homes. At the Golds', 19-year-old Paul (Joshua Jackson) has been in a coma for some time following a car accident. His mom, Esther (Close), is neglecting teen daughter Julie (Jessica Campbell) and her husband (Robert Klein), so intent is she on talking to Paul, even propping him up at the dining room table in hopes he will respond and return to consciousness.

Devastated after her husband left her, Annette Jennings (Patricia Clarkson) foolishly began a flirtation with Paul and now looks across from her window to see him unmoving and bedridden. She's also reduced to begging her deadbeat ex to send support payments for her special-needs daughter Rayanne (Haylee Wanstall) and boyish looking Sam (Kristen Stewart).

Over at the Train household, dad Jim (Dermot Mulroney) walks out of his law firm without explanation after being named their lawyer of the year -- but not a partner. But he doesn't confide in his puzzled wife, Susan (Moira Kelly), or notice that 12-year-old Jake (Alex House) is fixating on his younger sister's Barbie-type doll as if it were a real-live girlfriend.

Helen Christianson (Mary Kay Place), meanwhile, mother to young Sally (Charlotte Arnold) and grown Bobby (Aaron Ashmore), is suddenly feeling very middle-aged and undesirable, despite her husband's attentions.

When Julie persuades her mom to enter a radio-sponsored endurance contest at the mall where the one who keeps both hands on an SUV the longest wins, lawyer Jim is inspired to cheer Esther on night and day, much to his wife's amazement. The long hours away from her son give Esther time to think about her own future as she confides to Jim that after the accident she prayed to God to let Paul live, but now thinks God has a wicked sense of humor.

Things do not go well when Annette's ex shows up, not wanting to pay his fair share but wanting to take only Sam, not her emotionally troubled sister, on a vacation. Sam soon turns up missing but it's not at all what Annette thinks.

Randy (Timothy Olyphant), the local handyman, sees in Sam a strong resemblance to the younger brother he lost in the car accident that he survived but that left Paul in a permanent coma.

Writer-director Rose Troche combines several stories from A.M. Holmes, fusing them into one neighborhood where coming-of-age and mid-life crises percolate just under the surface. By and large, the characters are three-dimensional and realistic as they cope with feelings of resentment, jealousy, denial, sexual insecurity and grief. We see snippets of their lives in sometimes jarring crosscuts but eventually the rhythm of the film settles down as we find out what guilty secrets some of them have been keeping.

A neighborhood picnic in the final scene suggests that the characters have matured or come to terms with their problems in positive ways. Two couples whose marriages were shaky are looking cozy again and the youngsters seem happier. And Paul's mom looks at peace, surely sad since he is dead, but now able to move on -- as she explained to him just before she suffocated him.

That scene, as a tearful Esther first tells Paul how much she loves him, presents euthanasia as a gift a mother has given to the rest of her family so they can be whole and move forward with the rest of their lives. Its sugar-coating of a deliberate killing is startling and makes the film's justification of murder completely unacceptable. The filmmaker has subtly scored points about not defining yourself solely by your job or your physical beauty, but this "solution" to a problem should be scorned by more than just the Catholic audience.

Due to its positive depiction of euthanasia, sexual situations with fleeting nudity, momentary violence and sporadic rough language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
